claims.text: Adjusting the ratios of tungsten, molybdenum, and tantalum in a refractory high-entropy alloy can improve its mechanical performance.
The composition adjustment can produce a 15% mechanical-performance improvement relative to the baseline alloy.
The composition adjustment can maintain thermal stability at temperatures above 1000°C.
The composition adjustment can maintain irradiation stability at neutron fluences above 10^22 neutrons/m^2.
The relevant refractory high-entropy alloys may have an FCC or BCC crystal structure.
Improved grain-boundary cohesion and reduced dislocation density lead to enhanced mechanical performance.
The optimized alloy will exhibit a 15% increase in yield strength relative to the baseline.
The optimized alloy will exhibit a 10% increase in ductility relative to the baseline.
Al0.1CoCrFeNi is an example of a conventional refractory high-entropy-alloy baseline.
The hypothesis is falsified if the optimized alloy improves either yield strength or ductility by less than 5% relative to the baseline.

contradictions.description: The headline hypothesis describes a single 15% improvement in mechanical performance, whereas the predicted outcome assigns different improvements to yield strength (15%) and ductility (10%).

The intervention concerns adjustment of W, Mo, and Ta ratios, but the stated Al0.1CoCrFeNi baseline contains none of those elements, so it is not a direct base composition for the proposed ratio adjustment.
